example (a b : ℝ) : 0 ≤ a - b ↔ b ≤ a := by simp --error
example (a b : ℝ) : 0 ≤ a - b ↔ b ≤ a := by rw [sub_nonneg] -- error
example (a b : ℝ) : 0 ≤ a - b ↔ b ≤ a := sub_nonneg -- ok

What is going on here?

class AddZero' (M : Type u_2) extends Zero M, Add M where

instance : AddZero' Int where
instance : AddMonoid' Int where

  0 ≤ a - b ↔ b ≤ a := sorry

@Kim Morrison WDYT?

Note that when using the set_option, the unification is solved because unification finds a stuck metavariable that it then decides to synthesize a value of:

[Meta.isDefEq.stuckMVar] found stuck MVar ?inst✝ : AddGroup ℝ
[Meta.synthInstance] ✅️ AddGroup ℝ ▶

And if you don't use the set_option, this doesn't happen.

Aha, I figured out a solution. If you write

attribute [instance_reducible] Zero.zero

I think I understand a bit better now what is going on in Weiyi Wang's example.

The unification algorithm decides whether to try to synthesize an instance metavariable by calling the function getStuckMVar?. This function searches for an instance metavariable in an expression by recursing into arguments of projection instances. In this case it is being called on Zero.zero, which contains a metavariable of type AddMonoid' Int. We want it to synthesize this metavariable with type class search, so that the unification can then succeed.

The reason why this worked originally is that unification would unfold Zero.zero into the projection .1, and the call getStuckMVar? on that. Since getStuckMVar? does recurse into all projections, it does find the metavariable that we want it to find. But now, since Zero.zero isn't unfolded, getStuckMVar? doesn't find the required metavariable.

I also have a local "fix" which makes getStuckMVar? more correct (such that it can recurse more effectively and report things that actually block reduction) and also removes quite a few set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false ins but there's unfortunately many mathlib adaptations necessary (I'm not done lol). One of the common adaptations is what I've dubbed "CoeT explosion". Here's an example:

import Mathlib

variable (a b : ℝ) (ha : 0 < a) (hb : 0 < b) (h : a < b)

set_option trace.Meta.isDefEq true in
#check inv_strictAntiOn ha hb h

inv_strictAntiOn receives as a first parameter ?a ∈ Set.Ioi 0 and we provide 0 < a. You might think here: Well it does the reduction and the unifies ?a := a and everything is fine but no! You can see two defeq failures!

[Meta.isDefEq] ❌️ ?m.15 ∈ Set.Ioi 0 =?= 0 < a ▶
[Meta.isDefEq] ❌️ 0 < a =?= ?m.15 ∈ Set.Ioi 0 ▶

turns out it reduces too much on the Real side and then doesn't know what to do with the < from the Set.Ioi anymore because it's too generic. Now you might ask yourself: Why does it work then? Well, "CoeT explosion" it is:

[Meta.isDefEq] 💥️ CoeT (0 < a) ha (?m.15 ∈ Set.Ioi 0) =?= CoeT ?m.17 ?m.18 ?m.17 ▼
  [] ✅️ 0 < a =?= ?m.17 ▶
  [] ✅️ ha =?= ?m.18 ▶
  [] 💥️ ?m.15 ∈ Set.Ioi 0 =?= 0 < a ▼
    [] 💥️ ?m.15 ∈ Set.Ioi 0 =?= 0 < a ▼
      [] ❌️ @Membership.mem =?= @LT.lt
      [onFailure] 💥️ ?m.15 ∈ Set.Ioi 0 =?= 0 < a ▼
        [stuckMVar] found stuck MVar ?m.15 : ?m.11

CoeT fails because of a stuckMVar (which we don't find with my patch) and thus the term elaboration gets delayed in a similar way to by exact. Thus, many fixes involved adding smileys or by exacts to influence elaboration order.

This lemma in mathlib doesn't depend on anything else in mathlib:

universe u

theorem List.ofFn_get {α : Type u} : ∀ l : List α, ofFn (get l) = l
  | [] => rfl
  | a :: l => by
    rw [ofFn_succ]
    congr
    exact ofFn_get l

It fails unless the respectTransparency option is false, and it fails even if the implicit argument (f := (a :: l).get) is provided to ofFn_succ.

Tactic `rewrite` failed: Did not find an occurrence of the pattern
  ofFn (a :: l).get
in the target expression
  ofFn (a :: l).get = a :: l

where the top ofFn (a :: l).get has type (upon hovering)

@ofFn α (l.length + 1) (a :: l).get : List α

and the bottom one has type 

@ofFn α (a :: l).length (a :: l).get : List α

I feel like this is intentional? After all, (a :: l).length doesn't obviously look like _ + 1 so using this lemma there is technically defeq abuse; I guess that's one place where backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency actually makes sense to use.
But we are trying to remove respectTransparency. The two terms are definitionally equal, so something must be done with rw
If this is the intended new behavior, how would one fix the type mismatch in the expression? (A genuine question because I want to learn more technical skills in Lean)

Here's a detailed trace of how the inferInstanceAs leakage and the inv a := a⁻¹ eta-expansion interact to cause this failure, and why deleting the inv field fixes it.

The common setup:

FiniteResidueField K is a def (non-reducible), so it's opaque at reducibleAndInstances but unfolds at default. Its Field instance is:

noncomputable instance : Field (FiniteResidueField K) :=
  inferInstanceAs (Field (IsLocalRing.ResidueField _))

This tells Lean: "synthesize Field (IsLocalRing.ResidueField (FiniteElement K))." Lean finds the quotient field instance, which was elaborated with Quotient (...) as the carrier type. All its lambdas — including the inv function — have Quotient (...) as their binder domain:

inv = fun (x : Quotient (Submodule.quotientRel ...)) => [body]

This term is accepted as Field (FiniteResidueField K) because Quotient (...) =_def FiniteResidueField K at default transparency. The result is stored as-is — the binder domain is Quotient (...) in the actual Expr.

What checkInst compares:

checkInst compares two Inv (FiniteResidueField K) instances at reducibleAndInstances transparency:

  • LHS: (inferInstance : Inv (FiniteResidueField K)) — from Lean's instance search
  • RHS: Field.toGrindField.toInv — from the Grind.Field construction

The LHS goes through Field → DivisionRing → ... → Inv, bottoming out at @instFieldFiniteResidueField. Since instance projections are transparent at reducibleAndInstances, this reduces to the inv function stored inside that Field instance — the one with binder domain Quotient (...).

Scenario 1: inv a := a⁻¹ (fails)

Field.toGrindField has inv a := a⁻¹ in its with clause. When elaborated for FiniteResidueField K, this creates a new lambda:

fun (a : FiniteResidueField K) => @Inv.inv (FiniteResidueField K) instInv a

The binder domain is FiniteResidueField K because that's the type of a as written in inv a := a⁻¹.

This overrides the inv that would otherwise be inherited from ‹Field α›. The RHS Inv structure now contains this new lambda.

checkInst compares the inv fields:

  • LHS: fun (x : Quotient (...)) => [body₁]
  • RHS: fun (a : FiniteResidueField K) => @Inv.inv ... a

isDefEq at reducibleAndInstances first checks: are the binder domains equal? Quotient (...) vs FiniteResidueField K — FiniteResidueField is a non-reducible def, can't be unfolded → not defeq → fails.

Scenario 2: inv field deleted (succeeds)

Without inv a := a⁻¹, the inv field is inherited from ‹Field α› in the with clause:

{ CommRing.toGrindCommRing α, ‹Field α› with zpow := ..., ... }

The Inv component comes from ‹Field α›, which for FiniteResidueField K is @instFieldFiniteResidueField. The RHS inv field is the same function that was stored in the Field instance — the one with binder domain Quotient (...).

checkInst compares:

  • LHS: fun (x : Quotient (...)) => [body₁] (from instance search, through @instFieldFiniteResidueField)
  • RHS: fun (x : Quotient (...)) => [body₁] (inherited from the same @instFieldFiniteResidueField)

Both sides derive from the same Field instance via the same projection chain. At reducibleAndInstances transparency, instance projections are transparent, so both reduce to the same stored function with the same binder domain Quotient (...) → defeq succeeds.

The punchline:

Deleting inv a := a⁻¹ doesn't fix the inferInstanceAs leakage — the Quotient (...) binder domain is still there. What it does is ensure both sides of the comparison are consistently leaked: both use the same function with the same Quotient (...) domain, so they match. Writing inv a := a⁻¹ breaks the consistency by creating a fresh eta-expansion whose binder domain is FiniteResidueField K, introducing a mismatch that reducibleAndInstances can't resolve.

import Mathlib

set_option pp.explicit true

/--
trace: α : Type
P : α → Prop
a : @Subtype α P
⊢ @Eq (@Set.Elem α P) a a
-/
#guard_msgs in
example {α : Type} (P : α → Prop) (a : Subtype P) : a.val = a.val := by
  rewrite [SetCoe.ext_iff]
  trace_state
  rfl

After the rewrite tactic, the type of the equality in the goal is @Set.Elem α P. But Set.Elem takes a set as an argument, not a predicate, so this term is not well typed in the reducible transparency. Once such an inconsistency is introduced, things become very annoying, because a rewrite that looks like it should work now won't.

Here is the isDefEq trace leading to the bad term. m.9 : Set α ends up being assigned to p : α → Prop.

  [] ✅️ α =?= ?m.8 ▶
  [] ✅️ ↑a =?= ↑?m.10 ▼
    [] ✅️ a =?= ?m.10 ▶
    [] ✅️ α =?= α
    [] ❌️ P =?= fun x => x ∈ P ▶
    [] ✅️ a.1 =?= ?m.10.1 ▼
      [] a [nonassignable] =?= ?m.10 [assignable]
      [] ✅️ ↑?m.9 =?= Subtype P ▼
        [] ✅️ { x // x ∈ ?m.9 } =?= Subtype P ▼
          [] ✅️ fun x => x ∈ ?m.9 =?= P ▼
            [] ✅️ fun x => x ∈ ?m.9 =?= fun a => P a ▼
              [] ✅️ α =?= α
              [] ✅️ x ∈ ?m.9 =?= P x ▼
                [] ✅️ Set.instMembership.1 ?m.9 x =?= P x ▼
                  [] ✅️ Set.Mem ?m.9 x =?= P x ▼

Let me try to restate what I have understood from Joël's explanation. Saying that a functor is monoidal associates a data to some functor. Moreover, the composition of two monoidal functors is monoidal. So, if F, G, H are monoidal, then so are F ⋙ (G ⋙ H) and (F ⋙ G) ⋙ H. An important point is that the monoidal data associated to these two functors is different because it depends on the composition order. If you had F ⋙ (G ⋙ H) = (F ⋙ G) ⋙ H at instance transparency, this would give a diamond of the worse kind (i.e., non propositionally equal) because typeclass inference could choose the data from one composition order or the other. This is related to the "found messy" at the top of the message. Lean has special handling for so-called higher order output parameters and parameters that depend on them, and with respectTransparency false, transparency isn't bumped for such arguments and therefore stays at .reducible. The typical example is

class GetElem (coll : Type u) (idx : Type v) (elem : outParam (Type w))
    (valid : outParam (coll → idx → Prop)) where [...]

Here, valid is an output parameter and a function (i.e., higher-order). Being an output parameter, we expect it to be assigned by instance synthesis, and if possible we avoid assigning it by unification, because higher-order unification is a hard problem we can't solve efficiently. See ExprDefEq.lean for the docstring explaining this.

One of the places where these are handled specially is isDefEqArgs, which, when confronted with a problem like f a b =?= f d e compares a =?= d and b =?= e. For implicit arguments and instance arguments, transparency is bumped to implicit or default, depending on respectTransparency. But for the higher-order out parameters and their dependents, it looks like this:

    -- logic for the postponed higher-order arguments
    if respectTransparency && (implicitBump || finfo.paramInfo[i]!.isInstance) then
      unless (← withImplicitConfig <| Meta.isExprDefEqAux a₁ a₂) do return false
    else if !respectTransparency && finfo.paramInfo[i]!.isInstance then
      -- Old behavior
      unless (← withInferTypeConfig <| Meta.isExprDefEqAux a₁ a₂) do return false
    else
      unless (← Meta.isExprDefEqAux a₁ a₂) do return false -- <-- you are here!

In your example, the β : outParam <| α → Type is a function and an out parameter. Also you're disabling respectTransparency, so isDefEqArgs reaches the else branch. This the other branches call isExprDefEqAux inside withInferTypeConfig (bump to .implicit or .default) or withImplicitConfig (bump to .implicit), but not in this case.

Note that the example works if you enable respectTransparency true and make MyInt implicit-reducible. So there's a difference in the old and new behavior and I'm still in the process of finding out which behavior is the right one to have. This is a tricky corner of isDefEq.

I took at closer look at the necessity of NatIso.ofComponents. Take the example of whiskeringLeftCompEvaluation:

/-- Whiskering by `F` and then evaluating at `a` is the same as evaluating at `F.obj a`. -/
@[implicit_reducible, simps!]
def whiskeringLeftCompEvaluation (F : A ⥤ B) (a : A) :
    (whiskeringLeft A B C).obj F ⋙ (evaluation A C).obj a ≅ (evaluation B C).obj (F.obj a) :=
  NatIso.ofComponents fun _ ↦ Iso.refl _ -- was just `Iso.refl _` before

The expected type here is

(whiskeringLeft A B C).obj F ⋙ (evaluation A C).obj a ≅ (evaluation B C).obj (F.obj a)

The two sides are only definitionally equal if one can unfold the functor composition here.
Call the LHS L and the RHS R. The object components are, at implicit transparency:

L.obj G = ((evaluation A C).obj a).obj (F ⋙ G) = (F ⋙ G).obj a = G.obj (F.obj a)
R.obj G = ((evaluation B C).obj (F.obj a)).obj G = G.obj (F.obj a)

So these do match, but the map components are only defeq if Functor.comp can be unfolded. The important observation is that the data of the natural iso we want to construct doesn't depend on map at all. We can keep the object component of Iso.refl _, but we need to cast the naturality proof to the expected type. ofComponents does this by re-wrapping the natural isomorphism.

In order to make this automatic, I prototyped a cast_proofs% term elaborator, which allows to get rid of all the manual NatIso.ofComponents usages. The example above is mildly useful:

-   NatIso.ofComponents fun _ ↦ Iso.refl _
+  cast_proofs% (Iso.refl _)

It's more useful for more deeply nested situations like in pushforward₀CompToPresheaf:

-  NatIso.ofComponents
-    (fun M ↦ NatIso.ofComponents (fun X ↦ Iso.refl _) (fun f ↦ by
-      simp only [Iso.refl_hom, Functor.comp_obj, whiskeringLeft_obj_obj, Functor.comp_map]
-      rfl))
-    (fun φ ↦ by
-      ext X : 2
-      simp only [NatTrans.comp_app, Functor.comp_map, whiskeringLeft_obj_map, whiskerLeft_app]
-      rfl)
+  cast_proofs% (Iso.refl _)

Using this term elaborator, I just had to insert cast_proofs% in front of the original isos, whereever there was NatIso.ofComponents before.
